content: Chlorosis, also referred to as green sickness, is a type of anemia characterized by a greenish or pale tinge to the skin. Patients with this condition typically experience symptoms such as fatigue, shortness of breath, indigestion, headaches, an unpredictable or reduced appetite, and the absence of menstruation (amenorrhea). In modern medicine, this condition is recognized as hypochromic anemia. In 1554, Johannes Lange, a German physician, described chlorosis as a condition specific to young, unmarried women. He suggested that the cure involved engaging in sexual activity and conceiving, as he believed this would restore their health. The term chlorosis was introduced in 1615 by Jean Varande, a professor of medicine in Montpellier, deriving the name from the Greek word Chloris, which means greenish-yellow, pale green, or pallid. Both Lange and Varande attributed their understanding of the condition to the teachings of Hippocrates. Historically, chlorosis was also referred to as morbus virgineus (meaning virgin's disease) or febris amatoria (lover's fever). In 1811, Francis Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue defined green sickness as a condition affecting young women, attributed to prolonged celibacy. In 1681, Thomas Sydenham, an English physician, classified chlorosis as a hysterical disorder. He noted that it affected not only adolescent girls but also frail and slender women who appeared to be consumptive. Sydenham recommended iron as a treatment, describing its ability to invigorate the blood and stimulate the animal spirits, which he believed were weakened and suppressed. Similarly, in 1872, French physician Armand Trousseau advocated for the use of iron in treatment, though he also categorized chlorosis as a nervous disorder. In 1887, Andrew Clark, a physician at London Hospital, proposed a physiological explanation for chlorosis. He linked its occurrence to the physical demands of growth and the onset of menstruation in adolescent girls. Later, in 1895, Ralph Stockman, a pathologist at the University of Edinburgh, expanded on earlier research showing that inorganic iron played a role in hemoglobin production. Stockman demonstrated that chlorosis could be attributed to iron deficiency caused by menstrual blood loss and insufficient dietary intake. Despite Stockman’s findings and the proven efficacy of iron supplementation in alleviating symptoms, debates about the underlying cause of chlorosis persisted into the 1930s. Finally, in 1937, Arthur J. Patek and Clark W. Heath from Harvard Medical School concluded that chlorosis was, in fact, identical to hypochromic anemia, thereby resolving much of the historical ambiguity surrounding the condition.
